title: J. McIntyre Machinery, Ltd. v. Nicastro (2011)
summary: New Jersey lacked jurisdiction over a British machine maker on a record showing one confirmed New Jersey sale through an independent national distributor and no New Jersey-directed conduct; Kennedy’s four-Justice plurality demanded submission to the forum sovereign, while Breyer and Alito concurred only because an isolated sale failed under existing precedent.
notes:
The casebook discusses the difficulty of identifying the controlling rule in fragmented decisions. Do not label all of Justice Kennedy’s reasoning “the Court’s holding.”

Nicastro injured his hand on a metal-shearing machine made in England by J. McIntyre, which sold in the United States only through an independent Ohio-based exclusive distributor; the Kennedy plurality was joined by Roberts, Scalia and Thomas, and Breyer's concurrence (joined by Alito) rested on the thin record rather than the plurality's sovereignty theory.

sections.Parties: J. McIntyre Machinery, Ltd. (McIntyre UK), an English corporation that designed and manufactured metal-recycling machinery, was the defendant and petitioner. Robert Nicastro, a New Jersey worker injured by a McIntyre Model 640 Shear, sued individually and as administrator of the estate of Roseanne Nicastro. McIntyre Machinery America, Ltd., the independent exclusive United States distributor based in Ohio, and Curcio Scrap Metal, Nicastro’s employer and the machine’s purchaser, were separately owned participants below.
sections.Material Facts: On October 11, 2001 a three-ton Model 640 Shear severed four fingers from Nicastro’s right hand at Curcio Scrap Metal in Saddle Brook, New Jersey; he alleged that the shear lacked a safety guard. Curcio had seen the machine at a Las Vegas scrap-recycling convention in 1994 or 1995 and bought it from McIntyre America in 1995 for $24,900, shipped from Ohio. McIntyre UK had appointed McIntyre America its exclusive distributor for the whole United States; its officials attended annual industry conventions with the distributor in Chicago, Las Vegas, New Orleans, Orlando, San Diego and San Francisco, never in New Jersey. Its materials referred to United States safety standards. Discovery showed at most four machines in New Jersey and only the accident machine as a confirmed sale there, no New Jersey office, property, advertising or employees, and no regular flow of machines into the state.
sections.Procedural History: Nicastro sued in the Superior Court of New Jersey, Law Division, Bergen County, in September 2003 for defective design and inadequate warnings. The trial court dismissed for want of jurisdiction; the Appellate Division reversed and ordered jurisdictional discovery; the trial court dismissed again. The Appellate Division reversed a second time, 399 N.J. Super. 539 (2008), finding O’Connor’s stream-of-commerce-plus test met by the national distributorship, trade-show activity and design for United States standards. The New Jersey Supreme Court affirmed, 201 N.J. 48 (2010), holding a foreign manufacturer amenable when it knew or should have known that a nationwide distribution system might produce sales in any state and took no reasonable step to exclude New Jersey. The United States Supreme Court reversed 6–3 on June 27, 2011: Kennedy wrote for four (Roberts, Scalia, Thomas); Breyer, joined by Alito, concurred in the judgment; Ginsburg, joined by Sotomayor and Kagan, dissented.
sections.Issue: May New Jersey exercise specific personal jurisdiction over a British manufacturer in a products-liability action arising from a machine sold and causing injury in New Jersey, when the manufacturer cultivated the United States market through an independent national distributor and trade shows, the record shows one confirmed New Jersey sale, and no conduct was directed specifically at New Jersey?
sections.Holding: No, on this record. Justice Breyer’s concurrence, the narrowest ground supporting the judgment, held that one isolated sale, national marketing outside New Jersey and no regular flow of machines or New Jersey-specific effort failed to establish purposeful availment under World-Wide Volkswagen and the Asahi opinions; Nicastro bore the burden and proved a single sale. The plurality would require conduct showing an intent to invoke or benefit from New Jersey’s sovereign authority. Six Justices agreed that the record failed, and five (Breyer, Alito and the three dissenters) declined to adopt the plurality’s sovereignty theory.
sections.Reasoning: Kennedy’s plurality treated personal jurisdiction as a question of a sovereign’s lawful authority to bind a defendant, resting in an ordinary products case on purposeful availment of that sovereign’s benefits and protections. Because the suit was in state court the relevant sovereign was New Jersey, and McIntyre UK’s efforts to serve the United States as a national market did not show submission to New Jersey: the nationwide distributorship, conventions in other states and up to four New Jersey machines revealed a desire for American sales, but no New Jersey advertisement, visit, shipment, office or property invoked New Jersey law. Breyer found existing precedent sufficient: World-Wide Volkswagen rejected jurisdiction based on one product’s isolated arrival, the Asahi opinions identified a regular flow, additional forum-related conduct, or significant volume, value and hazard as what would count, and Nicastro proved none of them. He refused both the plurality’s sovereignty theory and New Jersey’s automatic nationwide-distribution rule, and declined to decide how the doctrine should treat nationwide or internet sales. The dissent saw a manufacturer that deliberately developed the whole United States market, so New Jersey was part of that market.

sources.label: Brief · Asahi, Nicastro and Burger King briefs, pp. 3–4

learning.why: New Jersey lacked jurisdiction on the record before the Court, but the six Justices supporting that result divided over how broadly to state the governing rule.

topics.cp-stream-commerce: A national distribution effort and isolated New Jersey sales did not produce a majority basis for jurisdiction.
topics.purposeful-availment: The plurality demanded purposeful affiliation with the particular state.
topics.cp-precedent: The concurrence agreed only on the narrower record and declined a sweeping rule for modern distribution.
topics.specific-jurisdiction: The case is a specific-jurisdiction decision about whether a single in-state sale suffices, and its fractured opinions shape how the arising-from inquiry is stated.
topics.cp-territorial: Kennedy's plurality framed jurisdiction as a question of sovereign authority and submission to a state's power, reviving territorial themes.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Breyer, joined by Justice Alito, concurred in the judgment on the thinness of the record alone and warned against announcing broad rules for modern distribution without a record presenting them. Justice Ginsburg, joined by Justices Sotomayor and Kagan, dissented: a manufacturer that targets the entire United States through an exclusive distributor should answer where its product is sold and injures a user, and the plurality’s rule lets it exploit the market while avoiding suit in any particular state.
